summary: Provides a general framework for describing network traffic flows and presents an architecture for measuring and reporting them. It explains how this fits into an overall flow architecture and how it can be used on the Internet. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes a system for measuring network traffic by grouping packets into flows and recording counts such as packets and bytes. It assigns separate roles to the devices that measure, collect, manage and analyze those records.

subtitle: A framework for grouping packets into flows and collecting network usage measurements.

tldr.problem: Network operators need consistent measurements of traffic use, performance and service, across different protocols and network platforms.
tldr.mechanism: Meters classify packet headers using rule sets and store flow records. Meter readers collect the records, managers configure the system, and analysis applications produce reports.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo describes an architecture rather than a protocol. It replaces RFC 2063 and leaves data-transfer mechanisms and record formats to other specifications.

today: RFC 2722 is an Informational architecture memo that obsoletes RFC 2063. It does not define a protocol for transferring usage records.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The Traffic Flow Measurement architecture defines common ways to describe network traffic flows and report measurements. Its address attributes are designed to apply across protocol stacks, and users choose what to measure by writing rule sets.

The collected data can help operators understand network behavior, plan growth, measure performance, check service quality and attribute traffic to users. This document is not a protocol specification; it structures the information a measurement system should collect and describes requirements and trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture gives different measurement systems a shared way to describe traffic. It says what information to collect, but not how to transmit that information between devices.

sections.title: Meters, Readers, Managers and Applications
sections.content:
A meter observes packet headers at a measurement point, classifies packets and accumulates attributes such as packet and byte counts. A meter reader collects usage data from one or more meters. A manager configures meters and controls readers, while an analysis application turns collected data into reports.

One manager should be the master of a meter and set meter-wide parameters. A reader is controlled by a single manager. Multiple meters or readers can provide redundancy, and collection times do not have to be synchronized.
sections.plainLanguage: Meters count traffic, readers collect those counts, and managers configure both. Analysis applications use the collected records to create reports.

sections.title: Flows, Attributes and Detail
sections.content:
A traffic flow is a measured portion of traffic with a start time and a stop time. Because IP packets are independent, a meter uses configured rules to decide which flow each packet belongs to. A flow record can include source and destination addresses, interface information, first and last times, and forward and reverse counts.

Granularity describes how much detail the rules preserve. More aggregation means fewer records and less overhead; finer detail means more individual flows. The RFC recommends rolling counters so later reports can retain totals after an earlier report is lost. Within one running rule set, each packet is counted in at most one flow.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow groups packets according to the meter's rules and stores measurements about that group. Operators can choose a broad grouping with fewer records or more detailed groupings with more records.

sections.title: How a Meter Classifies Packets
sections.content:
For each packet, the meter extracts attributes from its header and builds a match key. The Packet Matching Engine (PME) runs the current rule set against that key. The result is to ignore the packet, report no match, or produce a flow key used to locate or create a flow record.

Flows are bidirectional, so the meter may try the packet's addresses in reverse order if a forward match fails. A matching rule contains a test and an action. The RFC defines 17 PME opcodes; Rule set 1 is built into the meter and cannot be changed, while selecting rule set 0 stops measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: The meter checks each packet against its current rules and either ignores it or adds it to a flow record. If a packet does not match in one direction, the meter can try the reverse direction.

sections.title: Flow Records and Memory Pressure
sections.content:
Flow records can be INACTIVE, CURRENT or IDLE. The meter uses an inactive record for a new flow when possible; otherwise it can reuse an idle record. Before reclaiming an idle record, it should allow registered readers to collect the data, subject to the configured inactivity time and practical limits.

If flow-table use rises above a high-water mark, the meter should switch to a standby rule set that creates flows less quickly. A manager can collect more often or later switch back. The architecture does not define how usage records are transported from meter to reader; it gives SNMP with the Meter MIB as one example.
sections.plainLanguage: When the flow table is running short of space, the meter can use rules that group traffic more broadly. The manager can also increase how often a reader collects records.
